source.title: The Effect of Trap Color on Catches of Monochamus galloprovincialis and Three Most Numerous Non-Target Insect Species

method: field experiment: lured traps of six colours, catches per trap, GLMM with Dunnett comparison against white
conditions: Wild pine sawyers caught in the field in pure Scots pine stands (Poland, Międzychód and Wronki Forest Districts); cross-vane IBL-5 traps hung 4 to 6 m above ground, every trap baited with Galloprotect Pack lures, so the response is to coloured traps on a pheromone-kairomone lure, not to colour alone. Randomized complete block design, one trap of each colour per block, traps about 100 m apart; the text does not say how colours were placed within a block. Analysis: generalised linear mixed model with block as random factor, Wald chi-square for colour, Dunnett comparisons with the unpainted white reference trap, alpha 0.05. Trap counts are a capture outcome, so attraction, landing and retention are not separated, and no detection threshold is measured. 2020 experiment: 10 blocks in the two forest districts, traps set 29 to 30 June and checked 15 and 29 July; deep orange, light blue, pine green, jet black, pure white and unpainted white (the lower-reflection series). Colour effect on females chi2 = 36.6, df = 5, p < 0.0001; males chi2 = 15.6, df = 5, p = 0.0079; totals chi2 = 29.5, df = 5, p < 0.0001. In the same series female catches in light blue (5.3 +/- 1.12), pure white (5.6 +/- 1.15) and pine green (6.6 +/- 1.30) traps differed significantly from unpainted white, while jet black (8.9 +/- 1.61) was borderline (p = 0.0528); male catches differed only in pure white (1.5 +/- 0.46) and light blue (1.6 +/- 0.48). The 2019 series with other colours gave no significant difference (see the other record). Laboratory two-plate choice tests in the same paper are not used here.
quote: The unpainted white traps captured the highest numbers of females (14.0 ± 2.32 beetles/trap), males (4.7 ± 1.11 beetles/trap), and beetles of both sexes (18.6 ± 3.08 beetles/trap).

source.authors: Benjamin Henneberg, Torsten Meiners, Karsten Mody, Elisabeth Obermaier
source.title: Morphological and olfactory tree traits influence the susceptibility and suitability of the apple species Malus domestica and M. sylvestris to the florivorous weevil Anthonomus pomorum (Coleoptera: Curculionidae)

method: behavioural: still-air dual-choice olfactometer arena, apple twigs with blossom buds versus wire control
conditions: Adults collected from Malus domestica trees by limb-jarring in a botanical garden (post-diapause, mid-March to mid-April 2017), so field-collected, not naive and of unknown sex (sex not recorded). Still-air dual-choice arena (Petri dish with two pipette-tip holes 70 mm apart); stimulus a roughly 5 cm apple twig with 5 +/- 1 blossom buds against a wire model twig as control; 16 C, 70% RH; weevils food-deprived 24 h, acclimatised 90 min, observed 180 min, choice recorded at the end; each weevil used once, new twigs and clean dish per trial. Side randomisation or switching of twig positions is not reported, and the zone counted as a choice is not specified. One-sample chi-square tests. Control versus blank (n = 30) showed no preference (chi2 = 0.14, p = 0.71). Responsiveness 56 to 62% when a blossom-bud twig was offered, 23.3% for control versus blank, so many weevils made no choice. The paper's volatile table has internal inconsistencies, which do not affect these bioassays. n = 50 weevils per comparison.
quote: Weevils that were tested in bioassays for their preference for volatiles from apple blossom buds versus controls significantly preferred M. sylvestris (χ2 = 6.53; p = 0.01) but not M. domestica over the controls (χ2 = 0.57; p = 0.45).
note: Sentence read in two abutting pieces from the page, start and end confirmed. Authors from Crossref single-DOI lookup (four authors; CC BY 4.0, content-version unspecified; page prints the Creative Commons Attribution License); PeerJ page text gave only Henneberg et al. Volume 10, article e13566, no issue. Family and order from the printed title. Not on main (grep of peerj.13566: harvest-36 searched list only).

value: first choices at artificial flowers: strong preference for yellow over blue (p < 0.001)

source.authors: Kim C. Heuel, Tim A. Haßlberger, Manfred Ayasse, Hannah Burger
source.title: Floral Trait Preferences of Three Common wild Bee Species

method: behavioural: two-choice test with yellow versus blue cardboard artificial flowers, first approach per bee
conditions: Free-flying females of a ground-nesting aggregation in the Ulm University Botanical Garden, tested inside a mobile 1.5 m flight cage set above the nesting aggregation (the text does not say outright that the bees came from that aggregation); tests ran 8 am to 1 pm in May and August of 2022 and 2023. Two-choice test with artificial flowers (die-cut 3.3 cm cardboard disks) on green paper: wooden board with three flower pairs, 8 cm apart within a pair and at least 16 cm between pairs, board turned 90 degrees every 10 min, flowers renewed every 20 min; only the first choice of each female approaching the board (within 5 cm) was noted. Experiments were run when about 30 females were active in the cage and repeated three to four times for L. villosulum because of low participation; bees were not marked and some individuals may have taken part more than once, and the total number of bees tested is not given. Binomial GLMs with species as a fixed factor, then per-species models. Yellow cardboard colour angle 146 degrees, blue near maximum opposition in the bee colour hexagon; achromatic contrast against the green background similar but not identical (blue 0.217, yellow 0.234), so the authors note yellow's slightly higher contrast may add to the preference. The reflectance spectra are only in a supplement. In the same paper Osmia bicornis showed no hue preference (p = 0.339); that species and the commercially reared Bombus terrestris are not logged.
quote: Lasioglossum villosulum (p < 0.001) and B. terrestris (p < 0.001) both strongly preferred yellow over blue flowers.
note: Whole sentence read in one piece, start and end confirmed; the B. terrestris clause is not used for any value. Authors, title, volume 15, issue 6 and article 427 from a Crossref single-DOI lookup (CC BY 4.0, vor); page metadata lists CC BY 3.0. Family from the paper's own text (halictid bee, Figure 1 caption); order Hymenoptera from the main Halictidae row (Megalopta genalis), the page does not state it. Not on main (grep of insects15060427 and Lasioglossum villosulum).

value: no preference for a complex 12-compound floral scent mixture over simpler 4-compound mixtures at artificial flowers (p = 0.269)

source.authors: Kim C. Heuel, Tim A. Haßlberger, Manfred Ayasse, Hannah Burger
source.title: Floral Trait Preferences of Three Common wild Bee Species

method: behavioural: two-choice test with artificial flowers scented with a complex versus a simple volatile mixture, first approach per bee
conditions: Free-flying females of a ground-nesting aggregation in the Ulm University Botanical Garden, tested inside a mobile 1.5 m flight cage set above the nesting aggregation (the text does not say outright that the bees came from that aggregation); tests ran 8 am to 1 pm in May and August of 2022 and 2023. Two-choice test with artificial flowers (die-cut 3.3 cm cardboard disks) on green paper: wooden board with three flower pairs, 8 cm apart within a pair and at least 16 cm between pairs, board turned 90 degrees every 10 min, flowers renewed every 20 min; only the first choice of each female approaching the board (within 5 cm) was noted. Experiments were run when about 30 females were active in the cage and repeated three to four times for L. villosulum because of low participation; bees were not marked and some individuals may have taken part more than once, and the total number of bees tested is not given. Binomial GLMs with species as a fixed factor, then per-species models. Scent: a complex 12-compound mixture against each of three simple 4-compound mixtures, 30 microlitres (30 ng of substance) per flower, mixture as random factor. GC-EAD in the same paper: myrcene in mixture 3 elicited a response in 66% of the six L. villosulum antennae tested; most other compounds responded in all antennae. Colour, size and depth tests are separate records or not used. A null on a first-choice test with unreported total n cannot show that the bees could not tell the mixtures apart.
quote: We did not observe a general preference of any of the species for the complex mixture over the simple mixtures (O. bicornis: p = 0.429; L. villosulum: p = 0.269; B. terrestris: p = 0.197).
note: Sentence read in two abutting pieces, start and end confirmed; only the L. villosulum clause is the value. Bibliographic and licence notes as in the hue record. Family and order as in the hue record. Not on main.
